title: God is light (1 John 1:5–10)
hookLine: if we confess, he is faithful to forgive

cards: Walk into a dark room and flip on the light. The first thing you see is not the furniture. It's the mess: the clothes on the chair, the dust on the shelf, the mug you forgot.
In the dark, the room seemed fine. In the light, it's honest. That's why some of us prefer dim lighting.
Today's passage starts with a statement about God that is three words long in English, and then moves straight to what happens to our mess when that light comes on.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "God is light, and in him is no darkness at all." No shadows in the corners, nothing half-true.

teach.h: SAYING WE HAVE NO SIN: SELF-DECEIT.
teach.b: Then the conclusion: if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another. Light is also about honesty between people. Then a run of ifs, like doors.
If we say we have fellowship with God while walking in darkness, we lie. And: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."
The danger isn't having a mess; the letter takes for granted that there is one. The danger is saying there isn't.
Then the open door: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

teach.h: CONFESS: SAY THE SAME AS THE LIGHT.
teach.b: The Greek word for confess is built from same and say: to say the same thing, to agree. To confess is to finally say about your life what God already says about it, what the light already shows.
And the response isn't a lecture.
It's faithful and just. Faithful, because God keeps his promise to forgive.
Just, because the letter has just said that the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin. Churches practice confession differently.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess to God in the presence of a priest, in the sacrament of confession or reconciliation.
Many Protestants confess privately to God, or together in a prayer of confession during worship, and some confess to a trusted friend.

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians confess sins to God in the presence of a priest in the sacrament of confession; some Protestant services include a spoken prayer of confession, sometimes introduced with 1 John 1:8–9, followed by words of forgiveness.

o: a speech defending what you did and why
a list of rules you promise to keep from now on
saying honestly what the light already shows

games.q: the light comes on and shows something you've done wrong. according to 1 John, what's the open door?
o: confess it, and find God faithful to forgive.
games.why: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."

practice: Picture a lamp coming on in a room inside you, and let it shine on one thing you've done, or not done, that you've been avoiding.
Name it plainly, without excuses and without beating yourself up, saying the same thing the light says.
If you pray, say it to God and rest in the words faithful and just to forgive; if you don't, sit a moment in the relief of not pretending.

wordCard.voice: Confession. Saying the same thing about your life that the light already shows, and finding God faithful to forgive.

orig.note: Greek: to confess, literally to say the same thing (homos, same + legō, say).

carryVoice: Your line: faithful to forgive. The light shows the mess, and the door stays open. Rest well.
